'''Avalon Airport''' {{airport codes|AVV|YMAV}} is an [[international airport]], located in [[Avalon, Victoria|Avalon]] in the [[City of Greater Geelong]] in [[Victoria, Australia]]. While located outside the [[Melbourne]] metropolitan area, it is the second busiest of [[List of airports in the Melbourne area|the four airports serving the state capital]] in passenger traffic. It is located {{convert|15|km||abbr=on|0}} north-east of the [[Geelong city centre|Geelong CBD]] and {{convert|50|km|abbr=on|0}} south-west of the [[Melbourne central business district|Melbourne CBD]]. The airport is operated by Avalon Airport Australia Pty Ltd, a subsidiary of [[Linfox]].

Avalon is currently served by passenger airline [[Jetstar]], which began domestic flights in 2004.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.avalonairport.com.au/corporate/about-avalon/business-summary/|title=About Avalon|website=Avalonairport.com.au|access-date=18 August 2017|archive-date=28 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160828233819/http://www.avalonairport.com.au/corporate/about-avalon/business-summary/|url-status=dead}}</ref> The airport is also the site of the biennial [[Australian International Airshow]], which has been held at the venue since 1992.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.airshow.com.au/airshow2015/index.asp|title=HEROES OF THE SKY - AIRSHOW 2015 - AUSTRALIAN INTERNATIONAL AIRSHOW AND AEROSPACE & DEFENCE EXPOSITION - 24 February to 1 March 2015 GEELONG VICTORIA|website=Airshow.com.au|access-date=18 August 2017|archive-date=10 August 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170810135641/http://www.airshow.com.au/airshow2015/index.asp|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Unlike [[Melbourne Airport]], Avalon Airport is not governed by the Commonwealth's ''Airports Act 1996''. The airport has a single runway in addition to a helipad.

==History==
The airport is located on land of the original indigenous owners, the [[Wathaurong]] people,<ref>''From Duck Ponds to Lara,'' by Lara Heritage Festival Committee, 2004</ref> and a scatter stone area is preserved on the Avalon Airport site, out of respect for the original owners.<ref>Avalon Airport Environmental Strategy 2024-2028, section 7.2</ref> The land has undergone many changes over the past century.

In the beginning, the airport was a sheep and cattle farm and homestead, founded by James Austin, an immigrant from [[Glastonbury]], England. Austin established his farm and named the homestead "Avalon" after the isle of [[Avalon]] at Glastonbury, the mythical island in the [[Arthurian legend]]. In 1952 the Commonwealth Government bought {{convert|4333|acre|order=flip|abbr=on}} at Avalon for just £110, as the land was deemed to be of poor quality farmland due to the abundance of volcanic rock littering the surface.<ref>''From Duckponds to Lara,'' published by the Lara Heritage Festival, 2004, edited by Mary Budd, Caroline Delaney and John Grainger</ref>

The airport was opened in 1953, to cater for the production of military aircraft.<ref>{{cite press release|url=http://www.meinhardt.com.au/newsdeskdetail.php?nid=84 |title=Avalon Hangar Conversion for Qantas? Skybed Fit-Out Adds to Meinhardt Aviation Portfolio |date=10 December 2003 |publisher=Meinhardt |access-date=18 December 2007 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070829150256/http://www.meinhardt.com.au/newsdeskdetail.php?nid=84 |archive-date=29 August 2007 }}</ref> Previously, the [[Government Aircraft Factories]] at [[Fishermans Bend]], Melbourne had used a runway beside the factory. However, newer jet aircraft required a longer runway for safe operations, and the Fishermans Bend runway was being encroached upon by development.

A {{convert|10000|ft|abbr=on|0|order=flip}} runway was built by the [[Country Roads Board]], with the first plane landing on 3 April 1953 – a four-engined [[Avro Lincoln]] [[heavy bomber]] flown from Fishermans Bend. The [[English Electric Canberra]] [[light bomber]] was under construction at the same time at the new airport. In 1959, [[Qantas]] established a training base at the site.<ref>{{cite web|last=Fishwick|first=Bill|title=Qantas Boeing 707-138 Aircraft at Avalon Airport in 1959|url=http://www.adastron.com/707/qantas/avalon/avalon-2-bf.htm|work=VH-JET#1 & Her Sisters|publisher=adastron.com|access-date=2 April 2013}}</ref>

In 1961, Government Aircraft Factories combined with the Commonwealth Aircraft Corporation, and built and serviced 110 Mirage fighters at the site, and in 1970 Jindivik Target Aircraft transferred to Avalon Airport from Fishermans Bend, adding production of 170 Nomad and 75 Hornet military jets, in addition to servicing of other jets.{{citation needed|date=August 2021}}

In 1985, the Government Aircraft Factories changed its name to Aerospace Technologies of Australia (ASTA).<ref name=autogenerated2>[https://web.archive.org/web/20070609103735/http://www.boeing.com/global/Australia/History/gafASTA.html Government Aircraft Factories / Aerospace Technologies of Australia] [[Boeing]]</ref> Aircraft produced during this time included the [[GAF Jindivik]] [[Target drone|remotely piloted aircraft]], and [[GAF Nomad|Nomad]] civil aircraft. Under the ASTA banner, engines for the [[Dassault Mirage III]] jet fighters were produced, as well as assembly of the [[McDonnell Douglas F/A-18 Hornet|F/A-18]] [[multirole combat aircraft]] for the [[Royal Australian Air Force]] (RAAF).{{citation needed|date=August 2021}}

In 1990, ASTA acquired 99 year lease on the airport.<ref>ASTA acquires Avalon Airfield ''[[Australian Aviation]]'' issue 59 August 1990 page 6</ref> In 1996, the airport was sold to Foxerco, owned by [[Linfox]] and [[Serco]].<ref name=AFR25091996>[https://www.afr.com/companies/govt-closes-astaas-air-factory-19960925-k73j8 Govt closes ASTAAS air factory] ''[[Australian Financial Review]]'' 25 September 1996</ref><ref>Avalon sold and ASTAAS closed ''Australian Aviation'' issue 123 November 1996 page 6</ref>

In October 1988, the ASTA Aircraft Services division took the first [[Boeing 747]] to Avalon for [[Aircraft maintenance|servicing and maintenance]]. By December 1993, fifty 747 aircraft had been through the Avalon facility, and 820 people were employed at the site.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.dpc.vic.gov.au/domino/Web_Notes/pressrel.nsf/bfce938dc49fdcea4a2563710007b7b3/3811293f5a93c04f4a2561f10032a1e8!OpenDocument&Click= |title=AVALON LEADS THE WAY IN AEROSPACE, SAYS GUDE |access-date=23 July 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070928015703/http://www.dpc.vic.gov.au/domino/Web_Notes/pressrel.nsf/bfce938dc49fdcea4a2563710007b7b3/3811293f5a93c04f4a2561f10032a1e8%21OpenDocument%26Click%3D |archive-date=28 September 2007 |url-status=dead }}</ref> October 1995 saw a [[Cathay Pacific]] [[Lockheed L-1011 TriStar|Lockheed L-1011]] flown to Avalon for scrapping by ASTA Aircraft Services, in what was a one-off event.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.adastron.com/lockheed/oddities/oddities.htm|title= Oddities – The Lockheed File|publisher = Adastron|access-date=9 August 2009| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090912112129/http://www.adastron.com/lockheed/oddities/oddities.htm| archive-date= 12 September 2009 | url-status= live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.adastron.com/lockheed/oddities/vr-hof.htm|title=The Demise of TriStar VR-HOF – The Lockheed File|publisher=Adastron|access-date=9 August 2009| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090915031824/http://www.adastron.com/lockheed/oddities/vr-hof.htm| archive-date= 15 September 2009 | url-status= live}}</ref>

Training of pilots from Japan's [[All Nippon Airways]] commenced at the airport on 8 September 1993.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.dpc.vic.gov.au/domino/Web_Notes/pressrel.nsf/8c6a107c25fde2364a2562e600030477/3e8713d8fcdd9f544a2561f100308c23!OpenDocument&Click= |title=JAPANESE PILOTS' CAREERS SET FOR TAKE OFF AT AVALON |access-date=23 July 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930223304/http://www.dpc.vic.gov.au/domino/Web_Notes/pressrel.nsf/8c6a107c25fde2364a2562e600030477/3e8713d8fcdd9f544a2561f100308c23%21OpenDocument%26Click%3D |archive-date=30 September 2007 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

On 27 June 1995 Aerospace Technologies of Australia was [[Privatization|privatised]] by the [[Government of Australia|Federal Government]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/num_reg_es/sccfbr1995n349839.html|title=SUPERANNUATION (CSS) CONTINUING CONTRIBUTIONS FOR BENEFITS REGULATIONS (AMENDMENT) 1995 NO. 349|publisher = Commonwealth of Australia|access-date=23 July 2007}}</ref> selling the aircraft divisions to [[Boeing Australia|Rockwell Australia]], and the airport operations to Avalon Airport Geelong Pty Ltd.<ref name=autogenerated2 /> The ASTA airliner overhauling facility was closed in 1997.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://propertycouncil.gravitymax.com.au/nat/page.asp?622=276929&E_Page=17720 |title=Property Council of Australia — Geelong Fights Back |access-date=23 July 2007 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070928193915/http://propertycouncil.gravitymax.com.au/nat/page.asp?622=276929&E_Page=17720 |archive-date=28 September 2007 }}</ref>

The first scheduled passenger flights out of the airport were operated by [[Hazelton Airlines]], who commenced flights between Avalon Airport and [[Sydney Airport|Sydney]] in February 1995. 36-seat [[Saab 340]] aircraft were used for the service.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.dtf.vic.gov.au/domino/Web_Notes/pressrel.nsf/9d5a9280109520ff4a25620d002d06d8/a842a152df93919c4a2561f1003c209e!OpenDocument&Click= |title=GUDE WELCOMES GEELONG AIR LINK TO SYDNEY |access-date=23 July 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070928001636/http://www.dtf.vic.gov.au/domino/Web_Notes/pressrel.nsf/9d5a9280109520ff4a25620d002d06d8/a842a152df93919c4a2561f1003c209e%21OpenDocument%26Click%3D |archive-date=28 September 2007 |url-status=dead }}</ref> The service was discontinued after a short time due to a lack of passengers.{{citation needed|date=August 2021}}{{when|date=October 2021}}

[[File:Avalon-airport-hangars.jpg|thumb|1000px|center|Aircraft [[hangar]]s at the airport. The tail of VH-EBU ''Nalanji Dreaming'' can be seen in the second hangar.]]

===Post-privatisation===
Between 1997 and 2001 Linfox developed proposals to develop the land which formed the basis of the Avalon Airport Master Plan draft, 2013. In 1992, the airport began hosting the [[Australian International Airshow]].

On 1 June 2004, [[Jetstar]] started commercial flights from the airport, in addition to their operations at [[Melbourne Airport]].{{cn|date=July 2024}} In 2008, the Federal Government rejected an application to build an international terminal.<ref>International terminal at Avalon fails to fly ''Australian Aviation'' issue 252 August 2008 page 16</ref> 

In April 2010, [[Tigerair Australia]] announced it would base two aircraft and commence operations from Avalon later that year.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.traveller.com.au/tiger-airways-to-fly-out-of-avalon-so5v|author=Platt, Craig|title=Tiger Airways to fly out of Avalon|website=traveller.com.au|date=19 April 2010|access-date=15 August 2017}}</ref> By June 2011 however, Tigerair Australia announced it would be withdrawing several flights from Avalon, to be operated instead from Melbourne Airport.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.theaustralian.com.au/business/aviation/tiger-airways-moves-flights-from-avalon-to-tullamarine/story-e6frg95x-1226068504497|title=Tiger in Avalon-to-Tullamarine switch|date=3 June 2011|website=[[The Australian]]}}</ref> The remaining Tigerair Australia services were withdrawn after a series of incidents that led to airline's operations being suspended by the [[Civil Aviation Safety Authority]] the following month.{{cn|date=July 2024}}

In October 2012, the Federal Government announced that the airport's lease would be amended, allowing for the construction of a new terminal and the implementation of international flights. Avalon is the second airport in [[Victoria, Australia|Victoria]] to be designated as a [[port of entry]] for freight operations.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.theaustralian.com.au/business/aviation/avalon-airport-to-become-international/story-e6frg95x-1226494496597|title=Avalon airport to become international|date=12 October 2012|website=The Australian}}</ref>

In February 2022, [[Bonza]] announced that the airport would become one of its 17 destinations with the airline planning to fly to the Sunshine Coast from Avalon.<ref>{{cite web |date=15 February 2022 |title=Bonza Announces New Destinations |url=https://www.bay939.com.au/news/entertainment/131943-bonza-to-drop-bargain-flights-for-16-aussie-destinations |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220216103212/https://www.bay939.com.au/news/entertainment/131943-bonza-to-drop-bargain-flights-for-16-aussie-destinations |archive-date=16 February 2022 |access-date=16 February 2022 |website=[[Bay 93.9]]|language=en}}</ref> Bonza started commercial flights from the airport on 21 February 2023, in addition to their operations at Melbourne Airport.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flybonza.com/media/bonza-touches-down-in-victoria/|title=Sunshine Coast to Melbourne Avalon route launched today as Bonza makes its mark in Victoria|publisher=[[Bonza]]|date=21 February 2023|access-date=5 July 2023}}</ref> Bonza suspended all flights in early 2024.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Hall Chadwick Voluntary Administrators Update 14 May 2024 |url=https://www.flybonza.com/media/voluntary-administrators-update-14may2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240718032915/https://www.flybonza.com/media/voluntary-administrators-update-14may2024 |archive-date=2024-07-18 |access-date=2024-06-19 |website=Bonza}}</ref>

=== International flights ===
Avalon Airport served international flights between December 2018 and February 2020, until they were terminated due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic in Australia]]. 

Commencing 5 December 2018, [[AirAsia X]] [[Airbus A330]]s operated twice daily direct flights to [[Kuala Lumpur International Airport|Kuala Lumpur]], Malaysia from Avalon, shifting its operations from Melbourne Airport.<ref>AirAsia to transition its Melbourne services to Avalon Airport 5 December. AirAsia Newsroom, 10 July 2018.[https://newsroom.airasia.com/news/airasia-to-transition-its-melbourne-services-to-avalon-airport]</ref> The services were terminated during COVID, and reinstated out of Melbourne Airport in 2022.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.9news.com.au/world/airasia-x-flights-to-melbourne-sydney-perth-and-auckland-to-recommence/1afab680-9afc-42a9-bae7-faa6bd3db244 | title=AirAsia X to recommence flights to Melbourne, Sydney, Perth and Auckland | date=18 July 2022 }}</ref>
 
[[Citilink]] operated daily [[Airbus A320neo]] flights Avalon from to [[Ngurah Rai International Airport|Denpasar (Bali)]], Indonesia starting 24 January 2020.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.travelweekly-asia.com/Travel-News/Airline-News/New-direct-flights-to-Bali-from-Melbourne|title=New direct flights to Bali from Melbourne|website=www.travelweekly-asia.com}}</ref> They were terminated in late February 2020.<ref>{{Cite web |last=kojo |date=2020-06-26 |title=Avalon Airport responds to COVID-19 |url=https://www.linfox.com/avalon-airport-responds-to-covid-19/ |access-date=2026-04-25 |website=Linfox |language=en-AU}}</ref>

A media release on 22 October 2019 from the [[Premier of Victoria|Victorian Premier]]'s Office stated that [[VietJet Air]] was expected to begin flights from Avalon to Vietnam in the second half of 2020.<ref>[https://www.premier.vic.gov.au/vietjet-to-call-avalon-home-more-jobs-for-victoria/ VietJet To Call Avalon Home, More Jobs For Victoria]. Media release, Premier's Office. </ref> However, when VietJet commenced their flights to Melbourne in April 2023, they operated out of Melbourne Airport instead.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://global.vic.gov.au/news-events-and-resources/news/vietjet-to-commence-regular-flights-to-australia|title=VietJet launches regular flights between Melbourne & Ho Chi Minh City|publisher=Global Victoria, Victorian Government|date=19 May 2023|access-date=5 July 2023}}</ref>

In November 2025, Jetstar announced that they would commence flights to [[Ngurah Rai International Airport|Denpasar (Bali)]], Indonesia commencing 23 March 2026.<ref>{{Cite web |date=10 November 2025 |title=Jetstar invests in major Melbourne Avalon Airport expansion with direct flights to Bali and Adelaide and more low fares seats to Brisbane |url=https://newsroom.jetstar.com/jetstar-invests-in-major-melbourne-avalon-airport-expansion-with-direct-flights-to-bali-and-adelaide-and-more-low-fares-seats-to-brisbane/ |access-date=10 November 2025}}</ref>

===Future===
====Airport Master Plan 2015====
The Avalon Airport Master Plan was prepared by Avalon Airport Pty Ltd in September 2015 and was endorsed by the Department of Defence.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.geelongadvertiser.com.au/news/geelong/avalon-airport-gets-green-light-for-major-development/news-story/e520eb755bd76e92eaf4d5df5e02a96d|title=Avalon Airport gets green light for major development|newspaper=[[Geelong Advertiser]]|date=11 October 2015 }}</ref> The document provides for a significant expansion of the airport's operations, as well as the establishment of non-aviation related developments.

==Facilities==
{{Unreferencedsect|date=July 2024}}
Since the introduction of [[Jetstar]] in 2004, the Avalon Airport terminal facilities have expanded from the original size of {{convert|732|m2|sqft|abbr=on}} to nearly {{convert|5600|m2|sqft|abbr=on}}. Over $100 million has been invested in the airport thus far to complete the following:

* An apron expansion to accommodate a further four aircraft as well as enable the opportunity to accommodate an aircraft the size of a Boeing 747.
* A total of seven A320 sized aircraft can now be parked simultaneously in front of the airport terminal.
* Installation of a flight information display system
* Fuel farm expansion to triple storage capacity from {{convert|500000|to|1500000|L|USgal|abbr=on}} of A1 jet fuel plus installation of new fuel pipelines
* Construction of a new bus, taxi and hire car road and various rerouted roads to manage incoming passenger traffic and other road infrastructure upgrades
* Fuel farm electrical maintenance and demolition of unused buildings
* Significant infrastructure upgrades as part of the Australian International Airshow

=== Passenger terminal ===
The current terminal facility is approximately {{convert|4500|m2|sqft|abbr=on}} in area and houses four gates capable of servicing aircraft up to and including the size of the [[Airbus A321]]. In its present configuration, the terminal can accommodate around six domestic departures per hour. The airport has a total of eight aircraft parking bays; there are six on the Northern Apron and two on the Eastern Apron. On the Northern Apron, the airport can accommodate five Code C Aircraft ([[Boeing 737]] or [[Airbus A320]] aircraft) and one [[Boeing 747]].

Avalon Airport can accommodate two Boeing 747s or two [[Boeing 787]]s on the Eastern Apron. The Eastern Apron is also a remote parking bay which doubles as a freight bay. The airport is capable of fitting one [[Airbus A380]] at a time on the Eastern Apron; this means it can also accommodate the freighter version of the [[Boeing 747-8]], which is slightly smaller.

Currently the airport terminal is not equipped with [[aerobridges]], and does not feature any guest lounges.

===Freight facilities===
The most notable freight operations include the [[Australian Grand Prix]], [[Supercars Championship|Supercars]] and [[Superbikes]], plus some specialist charters including livestock race horses, fresh produce, military hardware and touring rock bands. The airport can facilitate loads on all aircraft types from the Airbus 380 series down, with equipment available to load via the main deck, lower deck, nose or tail end of the aircraft, with a maximum lift of {{convert|16|t|ST|abbr=on}}. It has three dedicated freighter parking positions: Two on its eastern and one on the northern freighter aprons.

===Aircraft heavy maintenance===
Avalon Airport has six hangars in total: {{convert|55000|m2|sqft|abbr=on}} of hangar space, including three customised ex-Qantas Boeing 747 hangars. The Qantas Engineering maintenance facility operated at the airport from May 1998 until its closure in March 2014.<ref>[https://www.theguardian.com/business/2013/nov/08/qantas-will-close-avalon-maintenance-base-with-loss-of-300-jobs Qantas will close Avalon maintenance base with loss of 300 jobs] ''The Guardian'' 8 November 2013</ref>

It was also responsible for the Qantas's aircraft commercial project work, including cabin reconfigurations and refurbishment.

==Other uses==
The video clip of [[Human Nature (band)|Human Nature]]'s 2000 song ''[[He Don't Love You]]'' was filmed at the airport.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OWMCEcFLQBw|title=Human Nature on Rove Live 2000|publisher=[[YouTube]]|work=hnfiwen|date=25 February 2011|accessdate=12 September 2022}}</ref>

In July 2013, it was proposed by Geelong City Council that a [[theme park]] be built at Avalon, and they have held discussions with [[Village Roadshow]] and other companies concerning the proposal. [[African Safari World]] was a previous proposal at nearby [[Werribee Open Range Zoo|Werribee Zoo]] that did not get approved.<ref>{{cite news|last=Fowles|first=Shane|title=Theme park being readied for takeoff at Avalon|url=http://www.geelongadvertiser.com.au/article/2013/07/25/369931_news.html|access-date=29 July 2013|work=Geelong Advertiser|location=Geelong|date=25 July 2013}}</ref>

The biennial [[Australian International Airshow]] operates from Avalon Airport. The project is owned by Aviation Development Australia Limited. The event attracts a total attendance of over 195,000 across the six days, including exhibitors from the international aerospace industry and government, military, scientific and trade delegates.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.airshow.net.au/airshow2013/index.html|title=AIRSHOW 2013 - AUSTRALIAN INTERNATIONAL AIRSHOW AND AEROSPACE & DEFENCE EXPOSITION - 26 February to 3 March 2013 GEELONG VICTORIA|website=Airshow.net.au|access-date=19 September 2013|archive-date=20 October 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131020221832/http://www.airshow.net.au/airshow2013/index.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Ground transport==
===Road===
Avalon Airport is linked to Geelong and Melbourne by the adjacent [[Princes Freeway]]. The airport has 1,500 airport car spaces, a taxi rank and a ride-share pick-up/drop-off bay.

===Public transport===
====Bus====
[[SkyBus (airport bus)|Skybus]] operates direct services to [[Southern Cross railway station|Southern Cross station]] in [[Melbourne central business district|Melbourne]], with an intermediate stop in [[Werribee]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.skybus.com.au/announcements/skybus-express-service-to-avalon-airport-commences|title=SkyBus is just the ticket as Victoria's second airport continues to grow|website=[[SkyBus (airport bus)|SkyBus]]}}</ref> Prior to Skybus commencing operations in 2017, the service was operated by [[Transit Systems Victoria|Sita Buslines]].<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20051124040223/http://www.sunbusaustralia.com.au/about_avalon.shtml About Sunbus: Avalon Airport] Sunbus</ref><ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20081220230801/http://www.sunbusaustralia.com.au/about_avalon.shtml Timetables: Melbourne to Avalon] Sunbus</ref>

Public bus services are operated to Avalon by [[CDC Geelong]] on behalf of [[Department of Transport and Planning|Transport Victoria]]. Route 18 runs between the airport and [[Lara railway station|Lara station]], providing a connection with [[V/Line]] trains to [[Geelong railway station|Geelong]] and Southern Cross via [[Sunshine railway station|Sunshine]].<ref>[https://timesnewsgroup.com.au/geelongtimes/news/two-year-fight-delivers-avalon-bus-service/ Two-year fight delivers Avalon bus service] ''Geelong Times'' 24 November 2025</ref><ref>[https://www.busnews.com.au/start-date-revealed-for-new-avalon-airport-seven-day-bus-service/ State date revealed for new Avalon Airport seven-day bus service] ''[[Australasian Bus & Coach]]'' 9 February 2026</ref> This service commenced on 15 March 2026.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Route 18 Lara Station to Avalon Airport Via Princes Fwy (From 15th March) |url=https://transport.vic.gov.au/route/timetable/,-w-, |access-date=2026-03-28 |website=[[Department of Transport and Planning|Transport Victoria]] |language=en}}</ref>

====Future rail connection====
In May 2011, the Victorian Minister for Public Transport committed $3 million for the planning of a rail link to Avalon Airport.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.premier.vic.gov.au/media-centre/media-releases/836-coalition-government-to-start-planning-avalon-rail-link.html|title=Coalition Government to start planning Avalon rail link - Premier of Victoria|date=20 September 2011|url-status=bot: unknown|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110920083552/http://www.premier.vic.gov.au/media-centre/media-releases/836-coalition-government-to-start-planning-avalon-rail-link.html|archive-date=20 September 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ausbt.com.au/avalon-to-become-second-melbourne-international-airport-with-rail-link|title=Avalon to become second Melbourne international airport, with rail link|website=Ausbt.com.au|date=5 May 2011 |access-date=18 August 2017}}</ref> In January 2013, three route options were presented. The railway line would start by running along the existing [[Warrnambool railway line]], and then divert towards Avalon Airport, south of Little River, at one of three locations. The eastern option would see the line break away closer to Melbourne, near Cherry Swamp Road and Little River. The central option would place the diversion {{convert|2.5|km|mi|abbr=on}} southwest, near Peak School Road at Lara. The western route option would divert from the existing line closer to Geelong, at Plains Road, Lara. Each of the three routes would run over the [[Princes Freeway]], north east of the Beach Road interchange at Little River, running under the flight path to a new station inside the terminal. The government would need to acquire private farmland to complete the link and is considering a number different options, including a light rail service or an automated driverless trains as used at several international airports.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.heraldsun.com.au/news/victoria/three-rail-choices-for-avalon-airport/story-e6frf7kx-1226564618266|title=Three rail choices for Avalon airport|website=[[Herald Sun]]|access-date=18 August 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.transport.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0008/85742/Avalon-Airport-Rail-Link_Phase-One-Investigations-Report_Appendices_C.pdf|title=Home|website=Transport.vic.gov.au|access-date=18 August 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140318000244/http://www.transport.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0008/85742/Avalon-Airport-Rail-Link_Phase-One-Investigations-Report_Appendices_C.pdf|archive-date=18 March 2014|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.transport.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0009/85761/Avalon-Rail-Link-Project-update-Jan-2013.pdf|title=Home|website=Transport.vic.gov.au|access-date=18 August 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140318000025/http://www.transport.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0009/85761/Avalon-Rail-Link-Project-update-Jan-2013.pdf|archive-date=18 March 2014|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In August 2013, the state government indicated that it may alter its election promise to build the $250 million railway line to Avalon Airport, and instead create a cheaper [[light rail]] link from Melbourne's south-west. Department documents show the government is now considering other options to meet interim demand, such as light rail, buses, or "driverless transport options which are used at many airports around the world".<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.theage.com.au/victoria/coalition-may-shift-to-avalon-light-rail-link-20130803-2r6bw.html|title=Coalition may shift to Avalon light rail link|first=Farrah|last=Tomazin|date=4 August 2013|work=[[The Age]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://s3-ap-southeast-2.amazonaws.com/ptvic/NDPMR+-+Network+Development+Plan+-+Metropolitan+Rail+-+FINAL+for+web+-+up.pdf|title=Network Development Plan – Metropolitan Rail|date=2 April 2014|url-status=bot: unknown|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140402032654/https://s3-ap-southeast-2.amazonaws.com/ptvic/NDPMR+-+Network+Development+Plan+-+Metropolitan+Rail+-+FINAL+for+web+-+up.pdf|archive-date=2 April 2014}}</ref>

In September 2023, Avalon Airport called for an alternate plan which would see an infill airport station built along the existing Geelong line, with a new road for shuttle buses to connect it directly with the airport.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=2023-09-19 |title=Avalon Airport CEO Tony Brun calls for $140 million rail link |url=https://www.abc.net.au/listen/programs/melbourne-drive/avalon-airport-ceo-wants-a-rail-link/102876210 |access-date=2023-09-20 |website=ABC listen |language=en-AU}}</ref> The plan was costed at $140 million with Avalon Airport CEO Tony Brun proposing to split the cost three ways between the airport, the state and federal governments.<ref name=":0" />

In May 2024, due to delays with the construction of the [[Melbourne Airport Rail]] link, State Treasurer [[Tim Pallas]] suggested that Avalon Airport could receive funding for a new rail link instead if Melbourne Airport is unable to agree on its station design.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kolovos |first=Benita |date=8 May 2024|title=Victorian treasurer threatens to consider train station for Avalon amid dispute with Melbourne Airport |url=https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/article/2024/may/08/victorian-treasurer-threatens-to-consider-train-station-for-avalon-amid-dispute-with-melbourne-airport |access-date=12 May 2024|website=[[The Guardian]]|language=en}}</ref>


==Accidents and incidents==
*On 6 August 1976, a prototype [[GAF Nomad|N24 Nomad]] crashed shortly after takeoff at Avalon while conducting a flight test of modifications to the tail of the aircraft. Two of the three crew members were killed in the accident,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://aviation-safety.net/database/record.php?id=19760806-0|title=Accident description:VH-SUZ 6 August 1976|publisher=Aviation Safety Network|access-date=15 August 2017}}</ref> notably including pilot Stuart Pearce, father of actor [[Guy Pearce]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/articles/3585|title=Government Aircraft Factories (GAF) Nomad|author=Crotty, D|publisher=Museums Victoria|access-date=15 August 2017}}</ref>
*On 30 June 2011, a [[Tiger Airways Australia]] [[Airbus A320]] flight from Sydney performed a [[missed approach]] at Avalon outside of published procedures, resulting in the aircraft overflying the Geelong suburb of [[Leopold, Victoria|Leopold]] at a dangerously low altitude, without guidance from Air Traffic Control. The incident made national headlines and triggered a five-week grounding of the airline over a busy school holiday period while a safety audit was conducted by the [[Civil Aviation Safety Authority]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.news.com.au/travel/travel-updates/tiger-flight-flew-low-without-clearance/news-story/d2f420ae70c227d63c96d049319e8b1c?from=newsverticalsyahoo_rss|author=Gardiner, Ashley|title=Tiger flight flew low without clearance, Australian Transport Safety Bureau finds|publisher=[[News.com.au]]|date=13 July 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine|url=http://blogs.crikey.com.au/planetalking/2013/12/18/safety-report-details-breach-that-got-tiger-airways-grounded/|title=Safety report details breach that got Tiger Airways grounded - Plane Talking|author=Sandilands, Ben|date=18 December 2013|magazine=[[Crikey]]}}</ref>

|issn=0261-3077}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=2025-03-06 |title=Boy charged after Avalon Airport shotgun incident |url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2025-03-06/avalon-airport-man-firearm-incident/105019482 |access-date=2025-03-06 |work=ABC News |language=en-AU}}</ref> The teenager threatened passengers and crew and Avalon Airport (IATA: AVV, ICAO: YMAV) is an international airport, located in Avalon in the City of Greater Geelong in Victoria, Australia. While located outside the Melbourne metropolitan area, it is the second busiest of the four airports serving the state capital in passenger traffic. It is located 15 km (9 mi) north-east of the Geelong CBD and 50 km (31 mi) south-west of the Melbourne CBD. The airport is operated by Avalon Airport Australia Pty Ltd, a subsidiary of Linfox.
Avalon is currently served by passenger airline Jetstar, which began domestic flights in 2004. The airport is also the site of the biennial Australian International Airshow, which has been held at the venue since 1992.
Unlike Melbourne Airport, Avalon Airport is not governed by the Commonwealth's Airports Act 1996. The airport has a single runway in addition to a helipad.
